questions.stem: In an ecosystem, what energy transformation do producers carry out in photosynthesis?
options: Heat energy from the sun into chemical energy in soil minerals
Light energy into heat energy that is stored in glucose
Light energy into chemical energy stored in organic compounds
Chemical energy in organic compounds into light energy
questions.explanation: Producers capture light energy and store it as chemical energy in organic compounds such as glucose. This chemical energy then passes to consumers through feeding. Heat cannot be used by producers to make organic compounds.

questions.stem: Why does energy flow through an ecosystem in one direction, while matter such as carbon is recycled?
options: Energy is eventually lost as heat, which organisms cannot turn back into chemical energy
Energy is destroyed at each trophic level when organisms carry out cellular respiration
Decomposers return energy to producers in the nutrients they release into the soil
Energy is stored permanently in the bodies of top predators and is never released to others
questions.explanation: At every trophic level, cellular respiration releases energy that is eventually lost as heat, and no organism can use heat to make organic compounds. Energy is not destroyed, only transformed. Decomposers return nutrients such as carbon and nitrogen, not energy, to producers.

questions.stem: As a young eucalypt grows, its dry mass increases greatly. Where does most of this added dry mass come from?
options: Carbon dioxide taken in from the air
Mineral ions absorbed from the soil
Organic matter absorbed by the roots
Water drawn up from the soil by roots
questions.explanation: Most of a plant's dry mass is carbon compounds made in photosynthesis from carbon dioxide in the air. This is how carbon enters biomass in the carbon cycle. Minerals make up only a small part of dry mass, and water is not counted in dry mass.

questions.stem: Producers in a grassland store 24 000 kJ per square metre per year in new biomass, and primary consumers store 2160 kJ per square metre per year. What is the efficiency of energy transfer between these levels?
questions.explanation: Efficiency = energy at the higher level ÷ energy at the lower level × 100 = 2160/24 000 × 100 = 9%. The value 91% is the share of energy not transferred, which is lost through respiration, waste and uneaten material.

questions.stem: Grasshoppers eat grass containing 1000 kJ. Of this, 600 kJ is lost in faeces and 300 kJ is released in cellular respiration. How much energy is available to the next trophic level?
options: 400 kJ, the energy absorbed through the grasshoppers' gut
300 kJ, the energy released by grasshopper respiration
700 kJ, the energy not used by grasshopper respiration
100 kJ, the energy stored as new grasshopper biomass
questions.explanation: Only energy stored in the grasshoppers' bodies as new biomass can pass to a predator: 1000 − 600 − 300 = 100 kJ. The 400 kJ absorbed includes the 300 kJ released in respiration, which is eventually lost as heat.

questions.stem: How is net primary productivity related to gross primary productivity?
options: Net productivity is gross productivity minus the energy producers use in respiration
Net productivity is gross productivity plus the energy eaten by primary consumers
Net productivity is gross productivity minus the energy lost by consumers as heat
Net productivity is gross productivity divided by the number of trophic levels present
questions.explanation: Gross primary productivity is the total rate at which producers store energy by photosynthesis. Producers use some of this in their own respiration, and what remains as new biomass, available to consumers, is net primary productivity.

questions.stem: Plants in a rainforest plot have a gross primary productivity of 30 000 kJ per square metre per year and use 18 000 kJ per square metre per year in respiration. What is their net primary productivity?
options: 30 000 kJ per square metre per year
12 000 kJ per square metre per year
48 000 kJ per square metre per year
18 000 kJ per square metre per year
questions.explanation: Net primary productivity = gross primary productivity − producer respiration = 30 000 − 18 000 = 12 000 kJ per square metre per year. Adding respiration to gross productivity, giving 48 000, reverses the relationship.

questions.stem: Only a small fraction of the sunlight reaching a leaf is converted into chemical energy. Which is the main reason?
options: Much of the light is reflected, passes through the leaf or is not absorbed by pigments
Most of the light energy is destroyed as soon as it strikes the surface of the leaf
Most of the light energy is used to pump water and mineral ions up from the roots
The leaf stores most of the light energy unchanged inside its cells for use later at night
questions.explanation: Some light is reflected from the leaf, some is transmitted through it, and some is of wavelengths that photosynthetic pigments do not absorb, so it is never captured. Energy is not destroyed, and light cannot be stored unchanged in cells.

questions.stem: One large eucalypt supports thousands of caterpillars, which are eaten by a few birds. What shape is the pyramid of numbers for this food chain?
options: Narrow at the base, wide in the middle and narrow at the top
Wide at the base and narrowing steadily towards the top
Narrow at the base and widening steadily towards the top
Wide at the base, narrow in the middle and wide at the top
questions.explanation: A pyramid of numbers counts individuals, so one producer gives a narrow base, the thousands of caterpillars a wide middle, and a few birds a narrow top. A pyramid of biomass or energy for the same chain would still be widest at the base.

questions.stem: In some oceans, the standing biomass of phytoplankton is less than that of the zooplankton that eat them, yet the pyramid of energy is still widest at the base. What explains this?
options: Pyramids of energy are measured at one instant, so they cannot show any turnover
Zooplankton lose no energy as heat, so their biomass builds up faster than it is eaten
Phytoplankton reproduce so fast that a small biomass produces a lot of energy over time
Zooplankton photosynthesise as well, so they need little energy from phytoplankton
questions.explanation: A biomass pyramid is a snapshot, and fast-dividing phytoplankton are eaten almost as fast as they grow, so their standing biomass can be small. A pyramid of energy shows energy flow over time, and because energy is lost at each transfer it can never be inverted.

questions.stem: Which process converts nitrogen gas from the atmosphere into ammonia?
options: Nitrification
Denitrification
Ammonification
Nitrogen fixation
questions.explanation: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria, including Rhizobium in legume root nodules, convert nitrogen gas into ammonia. Nitrification converts ammonium to nitrites and nitrates, and denitrification returns nitrates to nitrogen gas.

questions.stem: In the nitrogen cycle, nitrifying bacteria in the soil convert ammonium ions into:
options: nitrites and then nitrates
nitrogen gas and oxygen
amino acids and proteins
ammonia and then urea
questions.explanation: Nitrification is a two-step process in which one group of bacteria oxidises ammonium to nitrites and another oxidises nitrites to nitrates, which plants absorb. Conversion of nitrates to nitrogen gas is denitrification.

questions.stem: A paddock stays waterlogged for several weeks, and soil nitrate levels fall sharply. Which process most likely increased?
options: Nitrification by bacteria in the low-oxygen soil
Nitrogen fixation by bacteria in the root nodules
Ammonification by decomposers of dead plant matter
Denitrification by bacteria in the low-oxygen soil
questions.explanation: Waterlogged soil has little oxygen, which favours denitrifying bacteria that convert nitrates into nitrogen gas, so nitrogen is lost to the air. Nitrifying bacteria need oxygen, so nitrification slows in waterlogged soil.

questions.stem: Why do many farmers grow a legume such as clover or lucerne in a paddock before a cereal crop?
options: Legume roots release carbon dioxide that cereal crops then use in photosynthesis
Legumes convert soil nitrates into nitrogen gas, which cereal crops absorb
Bacteria in the legume's root nodules fix nitrogen, which enriches the soil
Legumes absorb nitrates from the air through their leaves and add them to soil
questions.explanation: Rhizobium bacteria living in legume root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia, which the plant uses. When the legume dies and decomposes, this nitrogen enters the soil and is available to the next crop. Plants cannot absorb nitrogen gas.

questions.stem: Which process returns carbon in dead organisms to the atmosphere?
options: Respiration by decomposers breaking down the dead matter
Photosynthesis by producers using the dead organic matter
Fossilisation of the dead matter over millions of years
Absorption of carbon dioxide into the surface of oceans
questions.explanation: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi feed on dead organic matter and release its carbon as carbon dioxide through cellular respiration. Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, and fossilisation locks carbon away.

questions.stem: Which part of the water cycle moves water from the soil into the atmosphere through plants?
options: Precipitation
Transpiration
Infiltration
Condensation
questions.explanation: Plants take up water from the soil through their roots, and most of it evaporates from their leaves through stomata, a process called transpiration. Infiltration is water soaking into the soil, and condensation forms clouds.

questions.stem: A clownfish lives among a sea anemone's stinging tentacles, which protect it, and it chases away fish that feed on the anemone. What type of interaction is this?
options: Parasitism
Competition
Mutualism
Commensalism
questions.explanation: Both species benefit: the clownfish gains protection and the anemone is defended from fish that eat it, so the interaction is mutualism. In commensalism only one species benefits and the other is unaffected.

questions.stem: Staghorn ferns grow on the branches of rainforest trees, reaching more light without taking water or nutrients from the tree. The tree is not affected. What interaction is this?
options: Predation
Commensalism
Mutualism
Parasitism
questions.explanation: The fern benefits by reaching light while the tree is neither helped nor harmed, which is commensalism. A parasite would take water or nutrients from the tree and harm it.

questions.stem: A paralysis tick feeds on a bandicoot's blood for several days and then drops off. The bandicoot is weakened but usually survives. What interaction is this?
options: Parasitism: the tick benefits at the host's expense, usually without killing it
Predation: the tick feeds on another animal and so must be its predator
Commensalism: the tick benefits while the bandicoot is unaffected
Mutualism: the tick benefits and the bandicoot gains lasting immunity
questions.explanation: A parasite lives on or in a host, benefiting at the host's expense, and usually does not kill it, at least not quickly. A predator kills and eats its prey. The bandicoot is harmed, so the interaction is not commensalism.

questions.stem: Two species of ant feed on the same seeds. When species A is removed from field plots, species B's numbers double; when species B is removed, species A's numbers rise. What interaction do these data indicate?
options: Predation of species B by species A
Commensalism, with species B benefiting
Competition between the two species
Mutualism between the two species
questions.explanation: Each species does better when the other is removed, so each is limited by the other's use of the shared resource, which is interspecific competition. If they were mutualists, removing one would harm the other.

questions.stem: In 30 quadrats, species Y is found only where species X is present and is most abundant where X is abundant. Species X occurs at similar densities whether or not Y is present. Which inference is best supported?
options: X and Y compete, since they are often found in the same quadrats
Y is a predator of X and keeps the numbers of X low in each quadrat
X and Y are mutualists, each needing the other in order to survive
Y benefits from X, while X is unaffected by Y, as in commensalism
questions.explanation: Y depends on X, but X's density is the same with or without Y, suggesting a one-sided benefit such as commensalism. Competition or predation would lower X where Y is common, and mutualism would make X depend on Y too.

questions.stem: What is an ecological niche?
options: A species' role in its ecosystem, including the resources it uses and its interactions
The physical place where a species lives, such as a rocky shore or a tall eucalypt forest
The position of a species in a classification such as the Linnaean hierarchy
The maximum number of individuals of a species that a habitat can support
questions.explanation: A niche is the role a species plays: the conditions it tolerates, the resources it uses, when and how it uses them, and its interactions with other species. The physical place where it lives is its habitat.

questions.stem: On a Scottish shore, Chthamalus barnacles normally live only on the upper rocks. When Balanus barnacles were removed from lower rocks, Chthamalus survived there too. What does the upper zone represent for Chthamalus?
options: Its fundamental niche, widened by mutualism with Balanus
Its realised niche, narrowed by competition with Balanus
Its fundamental niche, set only by its tolerance of drying
Its realised niche, widened by predation on the Balanus
questions.explanation: Chthamalus can survive lower down when Balanus is absent, so its fundamental niche includes the lower rocks. Competition from Balanus restricts it to the upper zone, its realised niche, the part of the fundamental niche it actually occupies.

questions.stem: What does the competitive exclusion principle state?
options: Two species using the same limiting resources cannot coexist indefinitely in one place
Two species using the same limiting resources will always evolve into one species over time
A predator always excludes its prey from the habitat in which the predator lives
Introduced species always exclude native species from the ecosystems they enter
questions.explanation: If two species have identical niches and resources are limited, the better competitor will eventually exclude the other from that area. Species can coexist only if their niches differ in some way.

questions.stem: Two Paramecium species each grow well when cultured alone. When cultured together on the same limited food, one species always dies out. What do these results support?
options: Mutualism between the two species
Exponential growth of both species
Commensalism between the two species
The competitive exclusion principle
questions.explanation: When two species with the same resource needs are grown together, the better competitor eliminates the other, as the competitive exclusion principle predicts. Mutualism or commensalism would not cause one species to die out.

questions.stem: Several warbler species feed on insects in the same conifer trees. Each species feeds mostly in a different part of the tree, such as the outer tips or the inner trunk. Why does this not contradict the competitive exclusion principle?
options: They use different parts of the resource, so their niches do not fully overlap
Competitive exclusion only applies to plants, which cannot move away from rivals
The insects are so plentiful that the warblers do not need to eat to survive
All the warblers belong to one species, so they cannot compete with each other
questions.explanation: By foraging in different zones, the warblers partition the resource, so their realised niches differ and they can coexist. Competitive exclusion applies only when niches overlap completely and resources are limiting.

questions.stem: What makes a species a keystone species?
options: It is a species that is found in only one ecosystem on Earth
Its effect on community structure is large relative to its abundance
It is the most abundant species in the community, measured by total biomass
It is always the producer at the base of every food chain present
questions.explanation: A keystone species has a disproportionately large effect on the structure of its community compared with its numbers, so its removal causes major changes. The most abundant species, or the main producer, is a dominant species, not necessarily a keystone species.

questions.stem: A predator eats three herbivore species. When the predator is fenced out of plots, one herbivore that is a strong competitor increases and the other two disappear. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The strong competitor is a keystone species, because it was able to increase most quickly
The predator is a keystone species that keeps diversity high by limiting the strong competitor
The predator lowers diversity, because removing it allowed one herbivore to increase in number
The three herbivores are mutualists, and losing the predator broke their mutual dependence
questions.explanation: With the predator present, the strong competitor is kept in check and all three herbivores coexist; without it, competitive exclusion removes two species. A species whose removal causes such a large change in community structure is a keystone species.

questions.stem: On a coral reef, one species of fish is the main grazer of the algae that grow on coral. Overfishing removes this fish. What is the most likely outcome?
options: Coral increases, because the fish no longer compete with it for sunlight
Algae decline, because the fish were their main source of nutrients
The reef is unchanged, because other fish increase to take its place
Algae overgrow the coral, reducing coral and the species that depend on it
questions.explanation: Without the grazer, algae are no longer kept in check and can smother coral, which loses the light it needs. Loss of coral then removes the habitat of many other reef species, a large change typical of losing a keystone species.

questions.stem: Which is an example of overexploitation?
options: Clearing native forest to create new grazing land
Planting a single crop over a very large area
Fertiliser running off farmland into a river
Harvesting a fish stock faster than it can reproduce
questions.explanation: Overexploitation is taking organisms from the wild faster than their populations can replace themselves. Clearing forest is habitat destruction, planting a single crop is a monoculture, and fertiliser runoff is pollution.

questions.stem: A diverse native grassland is replaced by a wheat monoculture. Why is the new community less stable?
options: Wheat plants carry out less photosynthesis than any native grass species
A monoculture has more trophic levels, so more energy is lost along the chain
A single crop species recycles nutrients faster than a mixed grassland can
Low diversity gives few food sources and habitats, and pests can spread easily
questions.explanation: A monoculture supports few species and few interactions, so there are fewer food sources and habitats for other organisms. With every plant the same species, a pest or disease can spread rapidly through the whole crop.

questions.stem: After fertiliser runs off farmland into a lake, an algal bloom forms. Weeks later many fish die. Which explanation is best supported?
options: The algae eat the small invertebrates that the fish rely on for their food
The algae photosynthesise so much that oxygen in the water reaches toxic levels
Bacteria decomposing the dead algae use up the oxygen dissolved in the water
The nitrates in the fertiliser poison the fish directly within a few weeks
questions.explanation: Extra nutrients cause rapid algal growth. When the algae die, decomposing bacteria respire and use up dissolved oxygen, and fish suffocate. This process is eutrophication.

questions.stem: Land clearing breaks a large forest into small, isolated patches. Why do some species disappear from the patches even though forest remains?
options: Forest patches always lose all of their producers within only a few years of clearing
Species in small patches stop reproducing until the forest is joined up again
Clearing removes every predator, so prey species outgrow their food supplies
Small patches support only small populations, and animals cannot move between them
questions.explanation: Habitat destruction and fragmentation leave populations that are small and isolated, with little gene flow, so they are more easily wiped out by chance events, disease or inbreeding. Some species also need larger areas than a patch provides.

questions.stem: What is the carrying capacity of an environment for a population?
options: The number of individuals that die each year from predation and disease
The largest population it can support in the long term with the resources available
The fastest rate at which the population is able to grow when its resources are unlimited
The total number of species that can live together in the same environment
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity is the maximum population size that the resources of an environment can sustain over time. It depends on biotic factors such as food and predators and abiotic factors such as water and climate.

questions.stem: A severe drought reduces pasture growth in a national park for two years. What is the most likely effect on the eastern grey kangaroos in the park?
options: Carrying capacity falls, so the kangaroo population grows exponentially
Carrying capacity falls, so the kangaroo population is likely to decline
Carrying capacity rises, because fewer competitors survive the drought
Carrying capacity is unchanged, as kangaroos can eat other kinds of food
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity depends on the resources available. Less pasture means less food, so the environment can support fewer kangaroos and numbers are likely to fall until conditions improve.

questions.stem: Which is an example of primary succession?
options: Recovery of a grassland after a flood deposits fresh silt
Colonisation of bare rock left behind by a retreating glacier
Regrowth of a eucalypt forest in the years after a bushfire
Weeds and shrubs growing on a cleared and abandoned farm
questions.explanation: Primary succession begins on a surface with no soil, such as bare rock, new lava or a fresh sand dune. After a fire, clearing or flood the soil remains, so recolonisation is secondary succession.

questions.stem: Why does secondary succession usually reach a mature community faster than primary succession?
options: Soil, seeds and roots remain, so plants can establish quickly
Pioneer species such as lichens grow faster after disturbance
There are no herbivores present to eat the young plants
Climate is always milder where secondary succession occurs
questions.explanation: In secondary succession the soil is already present and often contains seeds, roots and nutrients, so the slow stage of soil formation is skipped. Primary succession must start with pioneers that slowly weather rock and build soil.

questions.stem: Which features make lichens effective pioneer species on bare rock?
options: They grow slowly, produce a few large seeds and need deep, moist soil
They are large and long-lived and shade out all the competing species
They depend on other plants for nutrients and spread by underground roots
They tolerate drying and extremes, spread easily by wind and help form soil
questions.explanation: Pioneers must survive harsh, exposed conditions with no soil, disperse widely and reach new surfaces easily. Lichens release acids that weather rock and add organic matter as they die, beginning soil formation. Shade-tolerant, long-lived species arrive later.

questions.stem: Over 150 years after a glacier retreats, soil depth, plant biomass and species number all increase. Early colonists are small, fast-reproducing plants; later ones are large, long-lived trees. Which statement best explains the change in species?
options: Biomass falls as the community matures, which leaves bare space for trees to fill
Abiotic conditions stay constant, so species change only through chance arrivals
Early r-selected species improve the soil and shade, which favours K-selected species
Early K-selected species improve the soil and are then replaced by r-selected species
questions.explanation: Fast-growing r-selected pioneers modify the abiotic environment, building soil, adding nutrients and creating shade. These new conditions favour slower-growing, competitive K-selected species, which replace the pioneers. Biomass increases, rather than falls, during succession.

questions.stem: Two forest plots share the same climate and soil. Plot A, burnt 20 years ago, has a Simpson's index of 0.45 and biomass of 40 t/ha. Plot B, burnt 100 years ago, has an index of 0.78 and 210 t/ha. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Plot B must contain at least twice as many species as Plot A does
Diversity and biomass are higher where more time has passed since fire
Plot A is more diverse, because it was disturbed more recently by fire
Biomass falls as diversity rises during succession after a bushfire
questions.explanation: The older plot has both a higher diversity index and more biomass, consistent with succession increasing both over time. A Simpson's index reflects richness and evenness together, so it cannot show that one plot has twice as many species.
